title: Enzyme Biochemistry
objectives: Understand the structure and classification of enzymes
Describe the mechanisms of enzyme catalysis and kinetics
Analyze clinical applications and disorders related to enzymes

overview.title: Enzyme Overview
overview.content:
Enzymes are biological catalysts that accelerate chemical reactions by lowering activation energy without being consumed. Most enzymes are proteins (except ribozymes), and they exhibit extraordinary specificity and efficiency, with rate enhancements of 10⁶-10¹² fold over uncatalyzed reactions.

Key Characteristics

  • Catalytic Power: Accelerate reactions up to 10¹² times
  • Specificity: Absolute, group, and stereospecificity
  • Regulation: Allosteric control, covalent modification
  • Compartmentalization: Organized in metabolic pathways

Enzyme Classification

By Reaction Type (EC Numbers)

  • 1. Oxidoreductases (e.g., dehydrogenases)
  • 2. Transferases (e.g., kinases)
  • 3. Hydrolases (e.g., proteases)
  • 4. Lyases (e.g., decarboxylases)
  • 5. Isomerases (e.g., epimerases)
  • 6. Ligases (e.g., synthetases)

By Composition

  • Simple enzymes (protein only)
  • Conjugated enzymes (holoenzymes = apoenzyme + cofactor)

catalytic_mechanisms.title: Catalytic Mechanisms
catalytic_mechanisms.content:
Active Site Architecture

Features: 3D cleft with precise arrangement of functional groups

Catalytic Triad: e.g., Ser-His-Asp in chymotrypsin

Mechanistic Strategies

Acid-Base: Proton transfer (e.g., lysozyme Glu35)

Covalent: Transient intermediates (serine proteases)

Metal Ion: Zn²⁺ in carbonic anhydrase

Proximity/Orientation: Entropic advantage

Cofactors

Types: Metals (Fe²⁺, Mg²⁺), coenzymes (NAD⁺, FAD)

Vitamin-Derived: Thiamine (TPP), Riboflavin (FAD)

enzyme_kinetics.title: Enzyme Kinetics
enzyme_kinetics.content:
Michaelis-Menten

Equation: v = (Vₘₐₓ[S])/(Kₘ + [S])

Parameters: Kₘ (affinity), Vₘₐₓ (capacity), kₐₜ (turnover)

Lineweaver-Burk: Double reciprocal plot for analysis

Inhibition Types

Competitive: Increases apparent Kₘ (e.g., statins)

Non-competitive: Decreases Vₘₐₓ (heavy metals)

Uncompetitive: Binds ES complex

Mixed: Affects both Kₘ and Vₘₐₓ

Allosteric Kinetics

Sigmoidal Curves: Cooperative binding (e.g., hemoglobin)

Effectors: Homotropic (substrate), Heterotropic (regulators)

regulation.title: Regulation Mechanisms
regulation.content:
Covalent Modification

Phosphorylation: Kinases/phosphatases (e.g., glycogen metabolism)

Proteolytic Cleavage: Zymogen activation (trypsinogen → trypsin)

Allosteric Control

Feedback Inhibition: End-product regulation (e.g., CTP on ATCase)

Energy Charge: ATP/ADP/AMP ratios

Compartmentalization

Metabolic Channeling: TCA cycle enzymes in mitochondria

Isozymes: Tissue-specific forms (LDH, hexokinase)

clinical_applications.title: Clinical Applications
clinical_applications.content:
Diagnostic Enzymology

Markers: ALT (liver), CK (heart), PSA (prostate)

Isoenzyme Patterns: CK-MB for myocardial infarction

Enzyme Deficiencies

Lysosomal Storage: Gaucher's (glucocerebrosidase)

Inborn Errors: PKU (phenylalanine hydroxylase)

Therapeutics

Inhibitors: ACE inhibitors, protease inhibitors

Replacement: PEG-asparaginase for leukemia

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
Why do enzymes have optimal pH and temperature?+
pH affects ionization states of catalytic residues; temperature balances increased activity with protein denaturation. Most human enzymes work best at pH 7.4 and 37°C.
How does transition state stabilization lower activation energy?+
Enzymes bind the transition state tighter than substrates, distorting bonds and stabilizing high-energy intermediates through precise interactions.
What's the difference between Kₘ and Kₐₜ?+
Kₘ measures substrate affinity (lower = tighter binding), while kₐₜ (turnover number) is reactions per active site per second when saturated.
Why are multienzyme complexes evolutionarily advantageous?+
They prevent intermediate diffusion, minimize side reactions, and allow coordinated regulation (e.g., pyruvate dehydrogenase complex).
